results.title: Manus 2.0 AI Agents Expand the Product, but Trust Is the Real Test
results.content:
## Manus Studio Blends Generation With Direct Editing

Manus is betting that agents become more useful when users can inspect and edit their output without restarting the entire generation process.

The company has renamed and expanded its desktop experience as Manus Studio. It describes Studio as a shared workspace where people and AI can work on documents, spreadsheets, PDFs, presentations, websites, code, games, and video.

This design pushes against a recurring limitation of prompt-based creative tools. Generating an acceptable first draft can be fast, while correcting one specific element can become frustrating.

Manus illustrates the problem with video editing. A user might like an automatically generated advertisement but want to replace its music or use a different product image. [...] Regenerating the entire video could introduce new unwanted changes. Studio instead exposes clips, images, text, audio, and motion graphics as separate components on an editable timeline.

The user can make a direct change, then return the project to the agent for another pass. That creates a mixed workflow where manual editing and automated generation can alternate.

Manus says its Video Editor targets product advertisements, tutorials, vlogs, motion graphics, and AI-generated user-style content. The company specifies a focus on videos lasting 30 to 60 seconds.

The release also adds Alchemy mode, which combines video generation and code generation under an automated creative-direction process. Manus claims this mode improves composition, detail, motion, and pacing.

results.title: Introducing Video Editor in Manus 2.0: Anyone Can Now Make A Video Worth Posting
results.content:
## Part 2: Video Editor gives you the final cut

Manus usually gets the first version 80 to 90 percent there. But the last 10 to 20 percent is often what you care about most: the music a bit lower, a caption reworded, a shot half a second shorter, your own product photo instead of a generated one. These edits are small, but doing them only through chat is awkward. "Move it half a second earlier" is hard to say precisely, and fixing one thing can shift another. So we built Video Editor. It lives in Manus Studio, the Manus desktop app.

### Every layer is its own track [...] Manus 2.0 is out. For the past month, I’be been making videos with Manus almost every day. Launch films for new features, game trailers, news explainers, beat-synced animations, a last minute launch film for Cue that was requested the night before it went live. I even handed Manus the footage from a trip and let it do the editing, and was tempted to set up a scheduled task and have it make a new video every day on its own. Now that we’ve launched, I’d like to explain what I've learned in the past month while it’s still fresh. I will focus on two things: what Manus can do with video, and why, on top of that, we built Video Editor. The 52-second film below introduces the new video features. It was made by Manus, too. 

﻿ [...] Manus can make everything a video needs on the spot: shots from video models like Seedance 2.5, plus images, music, voiceover and sound effects. But what's special is the code. Manus has its own computer, enabling it to write code for motion graphics, layouts, charts and map routes, render them, screenshot the result to check it, and keep fixing what it doesn't like. I've watched it draw a grid over a frame in Python to locate pixels, and use FFmpeg to turn 24 fps footage into 120 fps so a 5x slow-motion shot stays smooth. I never taught it that. It worked these tricks out to make the video better. Generated shots and code-made visuals can share one video. For BEAT RUSH, Manus generated a dancing anime character with Seedance, then built the rhythm-game interface and beat effects in code.
